title: Variational quantum algorithm based on Lagrange polynomial encoding to solve differential equations
abstract_summary: The paper introduces two variational quantum algorithm (VQA) architectures that use Lagrange polynomial encoding together with derivative quantum circuits via the Hadamard test to approximate solutions of differential equations. The methods are evaluated on a damped mass–spring ordinary differential equation and the Poisson equation under various boundary conditions, and are shown in noise-free simulation to reduce gate complexity compared to prior VQAs (Kyriienko et al., Sato et al.) while achieving similar or improved solution quality.
methodology_description: The authors design and evaluate two new variational quantum algorithm (VQA) architectures for solving ordinary differential equations based on Lagrange-polynomial encoding of the independent variable and derivatives computed via Hadamard-test differentiation. Two circuit variants are presented: an "extended" multi-qubit encoding and a "simplified" single-ancilla encoding; both use a variational ansatz (hardware-efficient style simplified to RX + CNOT layers) applied to Lagrange-basis-encoded states and local Z measurements to read out interpolating polynomial values. They compare these new Hadamard-Lagrange VQAs against two baseline VQAs from the literature: a Kyriienko-inspired polynomial (Chebyshev) encoding approach (using parameter-shift differentiation) and the Sato et al. discretized Poisson VQA. Experiments are conducted in noise-free quantum-circuit simulation. The workflow: build encoding and variational circuits for training/evaluation points, evaluate function and its derivatives (parameter-shift or Hadamard-test depending on approach), compute a loss composed of mean-squared DE residuals plus boundary/initial-condition and optional regularization terms, calculate gradients w.r.t. variational parameters (parameter-shift rule) and update parameters with a classical optimizer (Adam, and BFGS used in the baseline). Convergence criteria include a target loss (e.g., 1e-4) or a component-wise gradient threshold (1e-4). Performance is assessed via (a) accuracy against analytical solutions (function and derivatives), (b) DE and boundary-condition loss contributions, and (c) gate/circuit complexity estimates (counts of basic gates and number of circuit evaluations). Two benchmark problems are solved: a damped mass-spring initial-value problem and the 1D Poisson equation under periodic/Dirichlet/Neumann boundary conditions.
algorithms_used: Kyriienko et al. algorithm (Chebyshev-encoding VQA) - used as baseline
Sato et al. algorithm (discretized Poisson VQA) - used as baseline
experimental_setup: All experiments were performed via noise-free quantum-circuit simulation (no real QPU). Circuits comprise Y- and X-rotation gates and CNOTs; measurements are projective Z measurements (local magnetization sums). Two circuit encodings were tested (extended multi-qubit and simplified single-ancilla Lagrange encodings). Training used sets of interpolation/training points (Chebyshev nodes and variants), and evaluation used 50 equispaced points for error assessment.

applications.name: Damped mass-spring system (IVP)
applications.equation: m d2f/dt2 + b df/dt + k f = 0
applications.training_point_selection: Chebyshev nodes (two variants: full Chebyshev nodes scaled to [0,0.9] and positive Chebyshev nodes scaled similarly)

experiment_process.overview: For each problem and algorithm: (1) choose training/interpolation points (Chebyshev or Lagrange nodes); (2) construct quantum feature-map encoding variable x (Chebyshev encoding for Kyriienko-inspired; Lagrange encoding with ϕ_i = arccos((x - x_i)/2) for Hadamard-Lagrange); (3) apply variational ansatz (RX rotations + CNOT layers) with trainable parameters θ; (4) evaluate function values by Z measurements, compute derivatives w.r.t. x (parameter-shift for Kyriienko; Hadamard-test differentiation for Hadamard-Lagrange) and assemble DE residuals; (5) compute loss = mean-square(DE residuals) + weighted boundary/initial-condition terms + optional regularization; (6) compute gradients w.r.t. θ (parameter-shift rule used) and update θ via Adam (LRs reported below) or BFGS for Sato baseline; (7) iterate until convergence criteria met (loss target or gradient thresholds). Additional Hadamard-Lagrange refinements: two-stage optimization with evolving training set and regularization (start with fewer nodes, add nodes after convergence on subsets), evolving learning rate (0.04→0.01 then 0.01).
experiment_process.convergence_criteria: Loss target ≈ 1e-4 or all gradient components below 1e-4
experiment_process.gradient_methods: Parameter-shift rule for parameter gradients; Hadamard test for derivatives w.r.t. x in new VQA
experiment_process.loss_components: DE mean-squared residuals averaged over M points; boundary/initial-condition MSE contributions; regularization points MSE (optional)

reproducibility_notes: The paper provides algorithmic descriptions, circuit structures (including encoding functions, ansatz structure), training procedures, loss definitions, and hyperparameter values (optimizers, learning rates, convergence thresholds, number of training/evaluation points). However, no code repository, software framework, simulator name, or exact script-level details (random seeds, full gate lists per run, exact initial parameter vectors) are provided. Reproduction is feasible in principle from the described methods but would require reimplementation of circuit constructions and the training loop; lack of public code or declared simulation environment reduces immediate reproducibility.
key_findings: [supported] Introduced two variational quantum algorithm (VQA) architectures ("extended" and "simplified") that use Lagrange polynomial encoding together with Hadamard-test-based differentiation to approximate solutions of differential equations.

[supported] In noiseless simulations for a damped mass-spring system (IVP), the Hadamard-Lagrange VQA achieved equal-or-better DE loss than a Kyriienko-inspired VQA and substantially better satisfaction of boundary/initial conditions (example DE losses reported: Kyriienko-inspired best 2.50e-3 and 2.77e-3; Hadamard-Lagrange 1.51e-3 and 2.87e-3 across two training sets; BC loss: Kyriienko-inspired 0.447 and 0.485; Hadamard-Lagrange 1.18e-3 and 1.07e-4).

[supported] For the Poisson equation (periodic, Dirichlet, Neumann BCs), the Hadamard-Lagrange VQA matched or outperformed the Sato et al. VQA on noiseless simulations; the authors report the Sato et al. mean absolute error was larger by factors ≈4× (periodic), 3× (Dirichlet), and 6× (Neumann) compared to Hadamard-Lagrange.

[supported] The Hadamard-Lagrange architecture required substantially fewer basic gates per iteration than the Sato et al. implementation in the authors' simulated tests (authors report ≈200× fewer basic gates per iteration for Hadamard-Lagrange vs Sato et al. in the Poisson test), leading to much lower estimated total gate counts in their experiments.

[supported] The two Hadamard-Lagrange structures are theoretically equivalent in noiseless simulation: the extended structure uses more qubits but fewer gates, the simplified structure uses fewer qubits at the cost of more gates; both yield the same theoretical output in the noiseless case.

[supported] Lagrange polynomial encoding with Hadamard-test-based differentiation produced smoother interpolants and reduced endpoint oscillations compared to the high-degree Chebyshev-polynomial encoding used in the Kyriienko-inspired method in the tested problems.

[supported] The Hadamard-Lagrange approach (with an evolving/paired training-and-regularization-point strategy) showed low sensitivity to random initialization of variational parameters in the reported runs, while the Kyriienko-inspired method showed higher sensitivity to initialization.
[supported] All experiments and comparisons reported were performed in noiseless circuit simulations; no noisy hardware results were presented.

[speculative] The authors suggest (but do not empirically demonstrate) that the Hadamard-Lagrange approach may be advantageous for NISQ devices due to reduced gate complexity and that either circuit variant might be preferable depending on device qubit-count vs gate-error tradeoffs.
[speculative] The authors propose that the approach could be extended to higher-dimensional PDEs and nonlinear differential equations but acknowledge this requires further work and testing.

[speculative] The paper argues (citing prior literature) that local Z-basis measurements and simpler Ansätze mitigate barren-plateau effects; this is presented as a motivation and design choice rather than being demonstrated extensively within this work.
results_summary: The paper presents two related VQA circuit architectures that encode Lagrange interpolation bases via a Hadamard-test-inspired feature map and use Hadamard-test differentiation for derivatives combined with parameter-shift gradients for variational parameters. In noiseless simulations the Hadamard-Lagrange designs produced smoother approximations and better boundary-condition adherence than a Kyriienko-inspired method on a damped mass-spring ODE, and matched or outperformed Sato et al.'s discretized VQA on a Poisson PDE while requiring far fewer estimated basic gates per iteration (~200× fewer in the reported Poisson test). Experiments were simulation-only (no noise) and the authors highlight trade-offs between qubit count and gate count across their two circuit variants and outline future work (higher dimensions, nonlinear DEs, testing on real hardware).
performance_claims: Hadamard-Lagrange achieved DE losses of 1.51e-3 and 2.87e-3 on two training-set variants for the damped mass-spring test (compared to Kyriienko-inspired best results 2.50e-3 and 2.77e-3).
Boundary-condition (BC) loss for Kyriienko-inspired runs: 0.447 and 0.485; BC loss for Hadamard-Lagrange: 1.18e-3 and 1.07e-4 in the corresponding tests.
In the Poisson equation tests, the Sato et al. algorithm's mean absolute error was reported as approximately 4× (periodic), 3× (Dirichlet), and 6× (Neumann) larger than the Hadamard-Lagrange result.
Authors report that Sato et al.'s circuit structure required roughly 200× more basic gates per iteration than the Hadamard-Lagrange circuit in the Poisson benchmark (simulation-based estimate).
Hadamard-Lagrange first-phase optimization averaged ~620–670 iterations (reported for two configurations) to converge to the first-stage criteria in the damped-mass-spring test.
To reach an equivalent averaged-in-space DE loss as Sato et al., the Hadamard-Lagrange run reached that level after ~300 iterations (reported in the Poisson test comparisons).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not claim or demonstrate a provable quantum computational advantage over classical methods. It reports reduced gate complexity and better or similar solution quality compared to two prior VQA proposals in noiseless simulation. Those are empirical improvements relative to other quantum ansätze in simulation, not demonstrated speedup or advantage over classical solvers or asymptotic scaling proofs.
limitations: Current fully quantum algorithms are limited by the need for large-scale, practical qRAM and by challenges in encoding/retrieving large classical data in superposition (author-stated).
Implementation on present hardware is constrained by noise, limited connectivity, limited qubit counts, and lack of fault-tolerant error correction (author-stated).

Variational quantum algorithms suffer from trainability issues such as barren plateaus and vanishing gradients; choice of cost function and circuit structure critically affect trainability (author-stated).

The Kyriienko algorithm was originally applied only to first-order DEs and requires extension/tuning to handle higher-order DEs; when applied to second-order DEs it exhibited oscillations and difficulty satisfying boundary conditions (author-stated).
The Sato et al. algorithm assumes the availability of an efficient unitary ˆUs to prepare particular source states, limiting applicability to arbitrary source terms (author-stated).
High-degree polynomial encodings (e.g., Chebyshev-based feature maps) can produce edge oscillations (Runge-like phenomena) and numerical instability for higher-order DE interpolation (author-stated).

Gate complexity: some VQAs (notably the Sato et al. and Kyriienko-inspired implementations) require substantially more gates and circuits per iteration, which may be prohibitive on NISQ devices (author-stated).

The Hadamard-Lagrange approach requires continuity of problem definitions (meshless, polynomial-fitting approaches), so discontinuities (e.g., in source terms) need special handling such as subdividing the domain (author-stated).
Estimates of gate complexity provided are order-of-magnitude and can be sensitive to initial parameter choices and optimizer behavior (author-stated).
The study and comparisons were performed in noise-free simulators; performance and tradeoffs (extended vs simplified circuit) on real noisy hardware remain unknown (author-stated).

[inferred] The Lagrange-encoding approach may face scalability limits because the polynomial degree (hence resource needs) scales with circuit size, possibly limiting applicability to large or high-resolution problems on NISQ machines.

[inferred] The simpliﬁed vs extended circuit trade-off (fewer qubits but more gates vs more qubits but fewer gates) introduces device-dependent vulnerabilities (gate error vs qubit decoherence/crosstalk) that are unresolved.

[inferred] The Hadamard-Lagrange encoding (linear/Lagrange polynomials) may not be optimal for strongly nonlinear PDE/ODE problems—choice of encoding could limit expressivity for some problem classes.

[inferred] Sensitivity to initialization of variational parameters (observed for Kyriienko-inspired circuits) indicates potential reproducibility and robustness issues depending on random seed and optimizer hyperparameters.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Introduces two VQA architectures (extended multi-qubit and simplified single-ancilla) using Lagrange-polynomial encoding + Hadamard-test differentiation that, in noise-free simulation, reduce gate/circuit complexity versus prior VQAs (Kyriienko et al., Sato et al.) while matching or improving solution accuracy on benchmark ODE/PDE problems.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Uses a hybrid quantum-classical training loop (variational ansatz on quantum circuits, classical optimizers Adam/BFGS and parameter-shift gradients) with two-stage optimization and evolving training node strategies to improve convergence.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Claims reduced circuit/gate counts and a simplified single-ancilla encoding that could make VQA-based differential-equation solvers more amenable to NISQ-era devices (argument supported by gate-count estimates from simulation).

#idea:quantum-advantage — Employs Hadamard-test differentiation to compute derivatives w.r.t. input variable x directly on circuit encodings, presented as advantageous relative to prior parameter-shift-only polynomial encodings for derivative evaluation.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Reports practical training details (learning-rate scheduling, Adam, gradient thresholds, two-stage node addition) highlighting the importance of classical algorithmic choices in VQA performance.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrates benchmarks on damped mass-spring ODE and 1D Poisson problems (various BCs) with quantitative error metrics (MSE, MAE, DE residuals) and iteration counts, showing feasibility at small qubit counts (example: 4 qubits in simplified setup).
